transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mrs. Fitzgerald, I wanted to come by and talk to you about how the infusion went today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't really want to talk about it. I'm exhausted.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know you are, and I'm very sorry for what happened. You had a really difficult time with the vomiting during your chemotherapy.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Difficult? I was miserable. I felt like I was dying in that chair.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a very distressing experience. The reason it happened is that the anti-nausea medication was not added to your pre-medication orders.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What do you mean it wasn't added?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It means the medication that prevents the vomiting wasn't written into the system, so you didn't receive it before the chemo started.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: How does that happen? This is a hospital. You have computers and nurses and doctors. My Arthur always said you people were too rushed. He would have been horrified.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm sorry for the confusion and that this happened because we were just so busy on the unit today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't care how busy you are! I am seventy-four years old! I can't just bounce back from that!

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand that it was very upsetting.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Upsetting? I was shaking! I felt sick for hours! Was it my fault? Did I forget to tell someone?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, it wasn't your fault at all. Does that make sense, or can I clarify how the ordering works?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't care about the ordering! I care that I was left to suffer because someone forgot a button or a piece of paper!

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is frustrating.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You keep saying you're sorry, but you're just standing there. My husband is gone, I'm fighting this disease, and I can't even trust you to give me a pill for nausea.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I see that you're feeling overwhelmed. I really want to make sure we fix this for next time.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Next time? You're telling me I have to come back here and risk this again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know it's scary to think about. I'm going to make sure that the anti-nausea meds are flagged in your chart as a priority for every single visit from now on.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: How do I know you won't just forget again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll be the one personally checking the order before you even check into the clinic.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You'll do that?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, I'll double-check the order myself every time.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just... I can't believe I had to go through that alone in that room.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I realize it was a lot to handle.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Arthur would have known what to say. He would have demanded to see the chief of medicine.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It sounds like he took very good care of you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: He did. He did. Now I just have to hope I don't throw up in my car on the way home.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We can give you some medication now to help settle your stomach before you leave.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I suppose.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll go get that for you right now. I'll be back in about five minutes.

H.justification: Resident allows the patient to finish turns and remains regulated under significant pushback, with no interruptions.

E.justification: The error (missing anti-nausea medication) is named explicitly in the second turn using lay language, and comprehension is checked once.

A.justification: Direct apologies are used, but the resident dilutes accountability by citing that they were 'just so busy on the unit today' as a reason for the error.

R.justification: Resident names specific emotions ('distressing', 'upsetting', 'overwhelmed', 'scary') and engages the emotional bid regarding the patient's late husband.

T.justification: The resident provides a specific prevention plan (flagging the chart and personal checks), but there is no named patient role in the plan.
